item.title: “To what extent, Venerable Gotama, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise?” -…
item.description:
“To what extent, Venerable Gotama, is the Dhamma visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise?” - “Brahmin, being infatuated by craving, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one plans for one’s own harm, plans for others’ harm, plans for the harm of both, and experiences mental suffering and mental distress. When craving is abandoned, one does not plan for one’s own harm, nor for others’ harm, nor for the harm of both, and does not experience mental suffering or mental distress. Being infatuated by craving, brahmin, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, misconduct of mind. When craving is abandoned, one does not engage in misconduct of body, speech, or mind. Being infatuated by craving, brahmin, overwhelmed, with mind obsessed, one does not know as it actually is one’s own benefit, nor the benefit of others, nor the benefit of both. When craving is abandoned, one knows as it actually is one’s own benefit, the benefit of others, and the benefit of both. Thus, brahmin, the Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.54

item.title: “Monks, when craving arises, where does it arise? When it establishes itself, where does it establish itself? Whatever in the world is endearing and agreeable:…
item.description:
“Monks, when craving arises, where does it arise? When it establishes itself, where does it establish itself? Whatever in the world is endearing and agreeable: In the world, the eye is endearing and agreeable. There this craving arises; there it establishes itself. The ear … the nose … the tongue … the body … the mind is endearing and agreeable. There this craving arises; there it establishes itself.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 22 – Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta

item.title: Life is swept along, The lifespan is short — Led to old age, There is no shelter. Seeing this danger in death, Always do meritorious…
item.description:
Life is swept along,
The lifespan is short —
Led to old age,
There is no shelter.
Seeing this danger in death,
Always do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.
Here, restraint of body,
Restraint of speech and mind —
One who does this, even while dying,
Experiences happiness,
Because while still alive,
He has made merit.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.51
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Rājadatta: A monk came to a charnel ground, Saw a woman’s body Abandoned there, Discarded in the cemetery, Food for worms. Some become disenchanted…
item.description:
Elder Rājadatta:

A monk came to a charnel ground,
Saw a woman’s body
Abandoned there,
Discarded in the cemetery,
Food for worms.

Some become disenchanted
Seeing such a miserable corpse.
In me, sensual desire arose —
Blind, I was bound.

Faster than boiling rice,
I left that place.
Mindful, clearly comprehending,
I came, sat to one side.

Then I attended to it,
Reflecting wisely —
The danger became clear,
I dwelt in disenchantment.

And my mind was liberated.
Seeing the Dhamma as it is,
I attained the three true knowledges,
Accomplishing the Buddha’s teaching.

From: Theragāthā 5.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Householder, suppose a man carries a blazing grass torch against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly let go…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose a man carries a blazing grass torch against the wind. What do you think, householder? If that man does not quickly let go of that blazing torch, could it burn his hand, his arm, or some part of his body, and would he thereby meet death or deadly suffering?” “Yes, venerable sir.” … “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a grass torch — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “But here, Udāyi, a person thinks: ‘Attachment is the source of suffering.’ Having known this, he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment.…
item.description:
“But here, Udāyi, a person thinks: ‘Attachment is the source of suffering.’ Having known this, he becomes unattached and liberated by the destruction of attachment. Udāyi, I say: ‘This person is not bound, not fettered.’ Why is that? Udāyi, the difference in his faculties has been fully understood by me.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 66 – Laṭukikopamasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Nun Mother of Abhayā: From the soles of the feet upward, From the top of the head downward — Contemplate this body — This…
item.description:
Elder Nun Mother of Abhayā:

From the soles of the feet upward,
From the top of the head downward —
Contemplate this body —
This body is truly impure,
Truly foul, stinking.

Thus abiding,
All sensual desire is uprooted.
Fever is abandoned —
I am cooled, at peace.

From: Therīgāthā 2.8
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, here a monk, reflecting wisely, does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to…
item.description:
“Monks, here a monk, reflecting wisely, does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … does not consent to arisen harmful thought; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes it non-existent. He does not consent to any arisen evil, unwholesome states; he abandons, dispels, destroys, makes them non-existent.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 2 – Sabbāsavasutta

item.title: “And how, good sirs, is one defiled by sensual lust? Here, good sirs, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is attached…
item.description:
“And how, good sirs, is one defiled by sensual lust? Here, good sirs, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is attached to agreeable forms and repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with bodily mindfulness unestablished, with a limited mind. He does not know as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are not abandoned without remainder. When he tastes a flavor with the tongue … When he cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he is attached to agreeable phenomena and repelled by disagreeable phenomena. He dwells with bodily mindfulness unestablished, with a limited mind. He does not know as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are not abandoned without remainder. This, good sirs, is called a monk who is defiled by sensual lust regarding forms cognizable by the eye … regarding tastes … regarding phenomena cognizable by the mind. A monk living thus, good sirs, if Māra approaches him through the eye, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object. If Māra approaches him through the tongue … through the mind, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.243
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Talapuṭa: O mind, everywhere, I have acted as you wished, For many lives — You were not angry with me, And this inner-born body…
item.description:
Elder Talapuṭa:

O mind, everywhere,
I have acted as you wished,
For many lives —
You were not angry with me,
And this inner-born body
Is your gratitude!
On the long path of saṃsāra,
Suffering was caused by you.

O mind, you yourself made
This person that I am —
You made me become
A brahmin,
A king, a royal,
One day a merchant,
Another day a servant,
Or a kind of deity —
All is due to you,
Made by you.

Due to your power,
We became asuras —
Due to you,
I fell to the bottom of hell;
Sometimes an animal,
Sometimes a hungry ghost —
All is due to you,
Made by you.

You will not deceive me
Again, many times more,
Like sorcerers
Performing magic tricks.
You played tricks on me,
Like playing with a madman.
O mind, tell me —
Where have I wronged you?

Formerly this mind wandered,
Went wherever it wished,
Went where it delighted,
Went where it enjoyed —
Now I will restrain it
With wise reflection,
As with a hook one restrains
A rutting elephant.

For me, the Teacher
Has declared that life is impermanent —
Life is not eternal,
Life has no core.
O mind, urge me
To leap into the Buddha’s teaching —
Make me cross the flood,
So very hard to cross.

I have now gone forth
In the Great Sage’s Dhamma —
Those like me
Do not accept loss.

Forests, oceans, rivers, land,
The four directions, above and below —
All are impermanent.
The three realms are perilous.
O mind, where will you go?
You will enjoy peace.

From: Theragāthā 19.1
📖 Read this sutta
